title: Safe Quoting and Argument Handling knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Safe Quoting and Argument Handling”?
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Quoting variable expansions” under lesson 130, “Safe Quoting and Argument Handling”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Safe Quoting and Argument Handling”?
options: Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
questions.answer_key: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
questions.explanation: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Safe Quoting and Argument Handling”?
options: Preserve values as separate arguments, quote expansions, and test inputs containing spaces or special characters.
Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
questions.answer_key: Preserve values as separate arguments, quote expansions, and test inputs containing spaces or special characters.
questions.explanation: Preserve values as separate arguments, quote expansions, and test inputs containing spaces or special characters. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
